764.title: The kingdom splits (1 Kings 12)
764.hook: Rehoboam ignores the elders' counsel, and ten tribes leave
764.howItsDone: Jews read the division of the kingdom in the book of Kings; from here the story follows two kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah, where David's house reigns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon's slow turning. Your line was even the wise drift. Did you turn one thing back a step? A new week begins, and Solomon's son faces his first test. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

A new king, a crowd, and a request. Solomon has died. His son Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has come to make him king. Their spokesmen don't waste words: your father made our yoke heavy. Lighten the hard service and the heavy yoke, and we will serve you. Rehoboam says, go away for three days, then come back. In those three days, he asks two groups for advice. Today's word is what happens after he chooses.
screen: `A CROWD AT SHECHEM.` → `LIGHTEN OUR YOKE.` → `COME BACK IN THREE DAYS.`

segments.voice: First Kings twelve. First Rehoboam goes to the old men, in Hebrew the zekenim, the elders who had stood before his father Solomon. Their advice is simple, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever." Serve them today, and they will serve you always. Then he goes to the young men who grew up with him. Their advice is the opposite. Tell them, they say, my little finger is thicker than my father's loins. My father chastised you with whips; I will chastise you with scorpions. Rehoboam goes with the young men. On the third day he gives the people the hard answer. And the people answer back with a cry: "to your tents, O Israel; now see to thine own house, David." The northern tribes walk away and make another man their king, and only Judah stays with the house of David. A prophet had already spoken of ten tribes torn away; now it happens. Look at what the elders actually said. Not be weak. Not give in on everything. Be a servant this day. One day of humility, for a lifetime of loyalty. They had stood before Solomon; they knew his reign from the inside. The young men had grown up at the new king's side. In this story the old counsel doesn't win because it's old. It carries weight because it came from people who had seen a reign from start to finish. Rehoboam had that advice in his hands, and he chose the voices that sounded like his own.
screen: `THE ELDERS: BE A SERVANT THIS DAY.` · `THE YOUNG MEN: WHIPS AND SCORPIONS.` · `TO YOUR TENTS, O ISRAEL.` · `COUNSEL FROM THE LONG RUN.` · then, large: `THEY WILL BE THY SERVANTS FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to an elder today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone older than you, or someone who has been at something longer than you have: a grandparent, a mentor, a neighbor, a colleague with decades behind them. What advice have they given you that you brushed aside? Or what question could you ask them that you haven't yet? Let their face come to mind clearly. If you pray, you can ask to know good counsel when it comes. Then plan one call or one conversation. The bell holds the time.
The kingdom splits. Rehoboam sets aside the elders' counsel to serve the people, and the northern tribes walk away. Today's word.
Your line: heed the old counsel. Today, ask someone who has seen the long run what they would do, and really weigh their answer. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

765.title: The ravens (1 Kings 17:1–6)
765.hook: in drought, ravens bring Elijah bread and meat
765.howItsDone: Jews read Elijah's story in the book of Kings, and Elijah appears in Jewish practice beyond it, as in the cup of Elijah set out at the Passover seder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kingdom split in two. Your line was heed the old counsel. Did you ask someone who has seen the long run? Today, a prophet walks onto the stage with almost no introduction. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

No family tree. No birth story. No call scene. Just a name and a place: Elijah the Tishbite, of the settlers of Gilead. He stands before King Ahab and says there will be no dew or rain in these years, except by his word. Then he leaves. God sends him to hide by a brook near the Jordan, in a land about to go dry. And the food that keeps him alive there comes from a source nobody would have picked. Today's word is the delivery.
screen: `ELIJAH THE TISHBITE.` → `NO DEW OR RAIN.` → `HIDE BY THE BROOK.`

segments.voice: First Kings seventeen. God tells Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith, near the Jordan. In the 1917 Jewish translation: "thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there." And they do. "And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook." The Hebrew word is orvim, ravens. And ravens, of all birds. In the Torah's list of birds Israel may not eat, the raven is there by name. And here it is carrying bread and meat to a prophet, morning and evening, in a drought. Some later commentators wondered whether orvim might mean people instead of birds. The plain story keeps the birds, and keeps the strangeness. Help arrives on the wings of something the Torah set apart as unfit for the table. There's a quieter point too. Elijah has just spoken a drought into the land. And the very next thing the text shows is that he has to be fed. He doesn't feed himself. He sits by a brook, waits, and accepts food from birds. One way to read it: after his big word, the prophet's next scene is about receiving. And it doesn't last: after a while, the text says, the brook dried up, because there had been no rain. He'll have to move on. But for a time the help came, twice a day, from the last place he'd have looked.
screen: `HIDE BY THE BROOK CHERITH.` · `ORVIM: RAVENS, ON THE TORAH'S LIST.` · `THE PROPHET HAS TO BE FED.` · `THE BROOK DRIES UP.` · then, large: `THE RAVENS BROUGHT HIM BREAD AND FLESH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept help from an unlikely place. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time someone helped you whom you didn't expect: a stranger, a person you had written off, someone you'd kept at arm's length. Let that face come to mind and stay a moment. Then look at today. Is there help being offered that you're refusing because of where it comes from? Pride, suspicion, an old story about that person. If you pray, you can give thanks for the ravens in your life. If you don't, just let the memory stay with you a while. The bell holds the time.
The ravens. Birds on the Torah's list of what not to eat, bringing bread and meat to Elijah by the brook, morning and evening. Today's word.
Your line: the ravens fed him. Today, if help comes from somewhere you didn't expect, say yes before you ask why. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

766.title: The widow's jar (1 Kings 17:8–16)
766.hook: a widow shares her last flour, and the jar never runs out
766.howItsDone: Jews read the story of the widow of Zarephath in the book of Kings, where it is followed in the same chapter by Elijah's prayer for her son.

segments.voice: Yesterday, birds brought Elijah his food by the brook. Your line was the ravens fed him. Did help come from somewhere you didn't expect? Today the brook is dry, and the help comes from someone with almost nothing. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

At the gate of a town called Zarephath, a woman is gathering sticks. Not many. Just enough for one small fire. A stranger, dusty from the road, calls out to her: bring me a little water in a vessel, so I can drink. She turns to go and get it. Then he calls after her again: and bring me, please, a piece of bread. She stops. Her answer is blunt, and it tells you everything about her kitchen. Today's word is in that kitchen.
screen: `THE GATE OF ZAREPHATH.` → `A LITTLE WATER, PLEASE.` → `AND A PIECE OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: First Kings seventeen. Zarephath belongs to Zidon, outside the land of Israel. She answers Elijah with an oath, as the LORD your God lives, and then the plain truth: she has nothing baked, only a handful of meal in a jar and a little oil in a cruse. She's gathering a couple of sticks, she says, to make one last meal for herself and her son, so that they can eat it and die. The Hebrew word for her jar is kad. Elijah says: don't be afraid. Go and do as you said, but make me a little cake first, and after that make some for yourself and your son. Because, he says, the LORD has said the jar of meal won't be used up and the cruse of oil won't fail until the day the LORD sends rain. Hear what he's asking. Her last flour. To a stranger. Before her own child. And she does it. The text says she, and he, and her house ate for many days, and in the 1917 Jewish translation: "The jar of meal was not spent, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD." Each day, she reaches into a jar that should be empty, and there's enough for that day. Not a mountain of flour. Enough. Notice who this miracle runs through. Not a king, not a priest. A widow in a town of Zidon, at the end of her supplies, who shares first. And notice how it follows yesterday. Ravens fed Elijah. Now a woman with nothing to spare feeds him. Giving, in this story, doesn't start with plenty. It starts with a handful.
screen: `A WIDOW IN ZAREPHATH OF ZIDON.` · `A HANDFUL OF MEAL, A LITTLE OIL.` · `MAKE ME A CAKE FIRST.` · `ENOUGH, EACH DAY, UNTIL THE RAIN.` · then, large: `NEITHER DID THE CRUSE OF OIL FAIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share from what little you have. Settle, and breathe. Name what feels scarce for you right now: time, money, energy, patience. Don't pretend it's plenty. Just name it honestly, the way the widow did at the gate. Now think of one small thing you could still share from it: ten minutes, a meal, a kind message, a few dollars. Not from the surplus. From the handful. Hold that thought and let it settle. If you pray, you can ask for some of her courage. The bell holds the time.
The widow's jar. A widow's last flour, shared with a stranger, and a jar of meal that didn't run out until the rain came back. Today's word.
Your line: the jar didn't fail. Today, share one small thing from what feels scarce, and see what's still there tomorrow. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

767.title: Between two opinions (1 Kings 18:21–39)
767.hook: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" on Mount Carmel
767.howItsDone: Jews read the contest on Mount Carmel as a haftarah, and at the close of Yom Kippur the congregation calls out the people's words from this chapter, that the Lord is God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow in Zarephath shared her last handful of flour, and the jar didn't fail. Did you share from the little you had? Today Elijah leaves the widow's house and climbs a mountain to face a whole people. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

Mount Carmel, and the slope is full of people. King Ahab has sent for all the children of Israel, and they've come up to watch a contest. On one side stand the prophets of Baal, the god Queen Jezebel favors. On the other side stands one man: Elijah. The land has had no rain for a long time. Before any fire is lit, before any altar is built, Elijah turns, not to the king and not to the prophets, but to the people watching. And he asks them a question.
screen: `ALL ISRAEL ON MOUNT CARMEL.` → `ONE MAN AND A CROWD.` → `A QUESTION FOR THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here is the question, in the King James words: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" To halt, in old English, is to limp. It's the image of someone hobbling, one foot on each side of a fork in the road, never quite walking down either. Then Elijah finishes the thought: if the Lord be God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him. And then the text gives the crowd's reply. The people answered him not a word. Silence. Nobody wants to choose. What follows is the contest. Two altars, two bulls, no fire. Whoever answers with fire is God. The prophets of Baal call out from morning until noon, and the text says, there was no voice, nor any that answered. Elijah rebuilds a broken altar of the Lord, has water poured over it until the trench runs full, and prays a short prayer. Fire falls and consumes everything, even the water in the trench. And now the people, who said not a word before, fall on their faces and say: "The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God." Remember that the question came before the fire. Elijah was after an end to the limping. In Jewish practice, the people's cry from this chapter returns at the very end of Yom Kippur, called out by the whole congregation as the gates of the day close. A people that once could not answer at all now answers together. The story keeps the uncomfortable middle part, too: the long silence, the people waiting to see who would win before they spoke. It doesn't pretend that choosing is easy. It only asks how long.
screen: `HOW LONG HALT YE?` · `THE PEOPLE ANSWERED NOT A WORD.` · then, large: `FIRE ON THE REBUILT ALTAR.` · then: `THE LORD, HE IS THE GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide one thing you've wavered on. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind something you've been limping on, one foot on each side: a call you keep almost making, a habit you keep almost dropping, a yes or a no you've left hanging. Small is fine. Notice what the waiting has cost: the energy of standing at the fork. Then, quietly, pick one side. You don't have to act on it this minute. Just let the decision land, the way the people's silence finally turned into words. If you pray, you can ask for clarity. The bell holds the time.
Between two opinions. Elijah's picture of a people limping at a fork, unwilling to walk down either road. Today's word.
Your line: how long between two opinions. Today, when you catch yourself hovering over a choice, ask it plainly, how long, and then take one step. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

768.title: Arise and eat (1 Kings 19:1–8)
768.hook: exhausted Elijah wants to die; an angel brings food and says "Arise and eat"
768.howItsDone: Jews read Elijah's flight to the wilderness as part of the book of Kings, and it is read in synagogue as a haftarah; the scene is often remembered as a picture of care for someone at the end of their strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on Mount Carmel, Elijah asked a silent crowd how long between two opinions. Did you settle one thing you'd been hovering over? Today, soon after the fire, the same prophet is running for his life. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

A message arrives from the palace. Queen Jezebel has heard what happened on Carmel, and she sends Elijah a promise: by this time tomorrow, you'll be dead. The man who stood alone against a mountain full of prophets doesn't stand this time. He runs. South, out of the kingdom, to Beer-sheba. He leaves his servant there and keeps going, alone, a day's journey into the wilderness. Then he sits down under a broom tree, a scrubby desert bush. And the prophet who faced down a whole mountain says he's done.
screen: `A THREAT FROM THE QUEEN.` → `A DAY INTO THE WILDERNESS.` → `UNDER A BROOM TREE.`

segments.voice: His words are blunt. It is enough. Now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am not better than my fathers. Then he lies down and falls asleep. Notice the timing. This isn't Elijah after a failure. It's Elijah right after Carmel. Fire fell from heaven at his word, and now he's under a bush asking to die. The text doesn't scold him for it. It doesn't call him weak or faithless. It just tells us what came next. An angel touches him and says: "Arise and eat." He looks, and there by his head is a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He eats, he drinks, and he lies back down. That's it. No lecture. No explanation of the big picture. Then the angel comes a second time, touches him again, and says it again: arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you. He gets up, eats, drinks, and in the strength of that food, the text says, he walks forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God. Look at the order. Before anyone talks to Elijah about his calling, his fear, or his future, someone feeds him and lets him sleep. Twice. The help comes as bread and water and rest. Some readers notice how tender this scene is: the God who sent fire on Carmel sends a meal under a bush. The great conversation is still coming, on the mountain. But first, the body. A tired person can't hear much of anything. So the first word from heaven is the plainest one possible. Get up. Eat something.
screen: `IT IS ENOUGH.` · `A CAKE AND A JAR OF WATER.` · then, large: `ARISE AND EAT.` · then: `THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat and rest when overwhelmed. Settle where you are. Ask your body a plain question: when did I last eat, drink water, or rest? Don't argue with the answer. Let your shoulders drop and your jaw loosen. Take a slow breath in and a longer breath out. If something heavy is pressing on you today, set it beside you for these two minutes, the way Elijah's journey waited while he slept. The decisions can wait for a fed and rested you. When the bell ends, if you can, get a glass of water or something small to eat. The bell holds the time.
Arise and eat. The angel's words to an exhausted Elijah under the broom tree, said twice, before any talk of what comes next. Today's word.
Your line: arise and eat. Today, when everything feels like too much, start with the simple things first: water, food, a few minutes of rest. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

769.title: A still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–13)
769.hook: not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but "a still small voice"
769.howItsDone: Jews read Elijah at Horeb as part of the book of Kings and as a haftarah, and the phrase kol demamah dakah appears in the Unetaneh Tokef prayer of the High Holy Days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, under the broom tree, an angel woke Elijah twice with the same words: arise and eat. Did you feed and rest yourself when it got heavy? Today, fed and rested, Elijah reaches the mountain. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

What doest thou here, Elijah? The question comes to him in a cave on Horeb, the mountain of God, where he has spent the night after a long walk. It's simple and direct. He has an answer ready. I have been very jealous for the Lord. The people have torn down your altars and killed your prophets, and I, even I only, am left, and they want my life too. It's the answer of someone who believes he is the last one left. And instead of an argument, he's told: go out, and stand on the mountain.
screen: `A CAVE ON HOREB.` → `WHAT DOEST THOU HERE, ELIJAH?` → `GO OUT AND STAND.`

segments.voice: What happens next is told in a careful rhythm. A great and strong wind tears at the mountains and breaks the rocks in pieces. "But the LORD was not in the wind." After the wind, an earthquake. But the Lord was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake, a fire. But the Lord was not in the fire. Three times the text builds up the noise, and three times it says: not there. And then, in the King James and the Jewish Publication Society words alike, "a still small voice." Elijah hears it, wraps his face in his cloak, and steps to the mouth of the cave. Remember who is standing there. This is the prophet of Carmel, the man of fire. Fire fell at his word. And now he's shown that God is not in the fire. The Hebrew phrase, kol demamah dakah, is hard to translate, and readers have heard it different ways: a still small voice, a quiet whisper, or even a sound of thin silence. The text doesn't settle it, and maybe the uncertainty is part of the point. Whatever it was, it was quiet enough that you could miss it if you were waiting for thunder. One more detail, and it's an honest one. The voice asks the very same question again: what doest thou here, Elijah? And Elijah gives the very same answer, word for word. The quiet doesn't magically fix him. But it's in that quiet that he receives his next instructions, and learns he is not as alone as he thought. The noise was real. The wind really did break rocks. It just wasn't where God was speaking.
screen: `NOT IN THE WIND.` · `NOT IN THE EARTHQUAKE, NOT IN THE FIRE.` · then, large: `A STILL SMALL VOICE.` · then: `THE SAME QUESTION, ASKED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in quiet. Put the phone face down, or out of reach. Close your eyes, or rest them on one spot. First, notice the loud things: traffic, a fan, voices, the noise in your own head. Don't fight them. Name them, one by one, and let each pass, the way the wind and the earthquake and the fire passed. Then listen underneath. The faint sounds: your breath, the room itself, a quiet you usually talk over. You're not waiting for anything to happen. Just stay at the mouth of the cave and listen. The bell holds the time.
A still small voice. What Elijah heard on Horeb after the wind, the earthquake and the fire: something so quiet it could be missed. Today's word.
Your line: a still small voice. Today, find one quiet minute away from the noise and listen for what you usually talk over. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

770.title: Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21)
770.hook: the king takes a man's land through false witnesses; Elijah confronts him
770.howItsDone: Jews read Naboth's vineyard as part of the book of Kings, and the story is remembered as a picture of a powerful ruler abusing the courts to take what belonged to an ordinary family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on Horeb, God was not in the wind or the fire but in a still small voice. Did you find a quiet minute to listen? Today that quiet prophet is sent back to the king, and he is anything but quiet. Day seven hundred seventy.

A vineyard in Jezreel, right next to the king's palace. It belongs to a man named Naboth. King Ahab wants it for a vegetable garden, and he makes what sounds like a fair offer: a better vineyard somewhere else, or its worth in money. Naboth says no. His answer, in the King James words: "The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee." This isn't stubbornness about real estate. In Israel's law, family land was an inheritance, meant to stay with the family. Ahab goes home, lies on his bed, turns his face to the wall, and won't eat.
screen: `A VINEYARD BY THE PALACE.` → `THE INHERITANCE OF MY FATHERS.` → `A KING SULKING ON HIS BED.`

segments.voice: Queen Jezebel finds him there. Are you the king of Israel or not? Get up and eat. I'll get you the vineyard. And she does, in a cold, careful way: with paperwork. She writes letters in Ahab's name, seals them with his seal, and sends them to the elders of Naboth's town. Call a fast. Seat Naboth at the head of the people. Then set two worthless men opposite him to testify that he cursed God and the king. The elders do exactly what the letters say. The false witnesses speak. Naboth is taken outside the city and stoned. And word comes back: Naboth is dead. Ahab gets up and goes down to take his vineyard. Notice how much of this looks legal. A public fast, witnesses, a trial, a sentence. Every step has a form. Only the truth is missing. And notice how many people went along: the elders, the nobles, the witnesses. The text records no one in the town saying no. Then, as Ahab walks into his new vineyard, Elijah is waiting. God sends him with one question for the king: "Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?" Two verbs, and they cut through all the paperwork. Ahab's reply is telling: "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" To him, the man naming the wrong is the enemy. The story doesn't end in neat justice that afternoon. Ahab humbles himself, and the punishment is delayed. But the question has been asked out loud, in the vineyard, to the king's face. This whole week we've watched a kingdom split, ravens feed a prophet, a widow's jar hold out, fire fall on Carmel, an angel bring bread, and a still small voice. Today the prophet's job is simplest of all: to speak for one man nobody else would speak for.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand up for someone wronged. Feet on the floor, one slow breath. Now think of someone who was treated unfairly, recently or long ago: a coworker blamed for someone else's mistake, a neighbor talked about behind their back, someone pushed aside because it was convenient. Notice who went along with it, maybe including you. Then think of one small, real thing you could do: a true word to the right person, a message of support, a refusal to repeat the story. Hold that one action in mind. The bell holds the time.
Naboth's vineyard. The family land a king wanted, taken through letters, false witnesses and a death, until a prophet named it. Today's word.

Your line: hast thou killed, and taken. Today, when something wrong is dressed up as proper, ask the plain question underneath it, and say one true word for the person it hurts. Day seven hundred seventy.
